lines: Thunder shook the forge so hard helmets rang on the racks, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked helmets and shields after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the forge, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the shield racks twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have shield racks to set right.
Lightning struck close enough to leave every buckle humming.
We moved people away from the windows before checking the racks.
One roof split under the rain, so the forge tarps went over a neighbor's bed.
The helmets stopped ringing before my hands stopped shaking.
I checked the square after every thunderclap for anyone caught outside.
Rain found three leaks above the armor stands. None were over a sleeping family.
The bell rope is soaked, but it still carried when we needed everyone indoors.
We kept the youngest villagers away from the chimney until the wind settled.
A shield cannot stop lightning. A sound roof and quick warning can.
The storm loosened tiles, shutters, and more nerves than I can count.
I put the repair list aside until every frightened neighbor had company.
The forge fire survived, though we lowered it when the roof began to shake.
Morning showed scorch marks on the well and no names missing from the village.
We are drying straps by the hearth and blankets beside them.
The next storm will find better braces on every exposed door.
I checked leather straps and coal bins for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the coal bin after.
Armor work can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the forge, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the forge, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
The bucket line mattered more than every tool hanging in my forge.
Smoke found the square before anyone saw the flames.
I pulled hot metal from the doorway so nobody tripped while carrying water.
We soaked blankets for the neighbors who had to cross the smoke.
The coal bin is cold now. I checked it with my own hands.
One burned roof can be rebuilt. A pair of lungs is harder to replace.
We kept helmets off anyone coughing so they could breathe freely.
The forge tongs carried embers out of reach instead of iron today.
I will smell smoke in the leather racks for weeks.
The last flame died before anyone dared stop passing water.
We marked every wall that stayed hot after the fire looked finished.
A child found shelter behind the smithy wall while the square cleared.
I am replacing scorched straps only after the displaced families have beds.
The village lost blocks and tools, but no one was left inside.
Tomorrow we rebuild with more stone around every open flame.
During a raid, armor can wait on the stand. Who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the forge still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before helmets and shields. That's the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the forge and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the forge, I saw fear cross the square. Then I saw courage get there first.
Every shield on the rack found an arm before the second horn.
We opened the forge doors for the wounded and barred them behind us.
The raiders tested our armor, but they tested our nerve harder.
I counted dents only after the last missing neighbor answered.
One breastplate split at the shoulder and still bought its wearer time to reach cover.
We dragged spare shields to the square while the bell kept ringing.
The road is quiet now, though nobody trusts the silence yet.
I saw villagers hold a doorway together when either one could have run.
The forge floor is covered in broken bolts and strips of bloody padding.
We are fitting the night watch before repairing anything meant for display.
A good helmet saved one life. A neighbor pulling them home saved the rest.
The raid showed every weak latch and every brave pair of hands.
I will mend the shields, but some of those frightened faces need gentler work.
We shared food beside the bell because no one wanted to eat alone.
If the horns return, the village will meet them behind stronger doors.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the forge first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the shield rack and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the forge enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a tightened shield strap between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the forge, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
We found claw marks on the forge door after sunrise.
Every loose latch is being replaced before darkness returns.
I kept spare shields by the square while the watch searched the alleys.
The lamps looked too small against that much dark, but they guided people home.
One villager spent the night under my workbench rather than cross the open road.
We listened for names between every noise outside the shutters.
Dawn found us exhausted and still counting one another.
The armor racks cast shadows that made everyone reach for a weapon twice.
We are trimming hedges and clearing anything that hid the approach.
The night watch will carry fitted helmets instead of whatever was nearest.
No one walks from the bell to the farms alone tonight.
A shield strap snapped while someone barred a door. I have already replaced it.
The attack ended, but sleep did not return with the silence.
We checked every house whose lantern went dark too early.
Tonight there will be more lamps, more watchers, and fewer blind corners.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning grit out of the visors.
I checked helmets and shields, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the forge, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches an armorer which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the forge, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
Grit reached every hinge in the forge and half the beds in the village.
We wrapped cloth over mouths before worrying about the armor racks.
The square vanished behind sand, so everyone followed the bell by sound.
I found three helmets packed so full of grit they could barely turn.
A door that rattles in ordinary wind becomes a danger in a storm like that.
We tied guide ropes between the forge, the well, and the nearest houses.
The youngest villagers slept away from the windows while boards shook outside.
I am oiling every clasp that the sand tried to lock shut.
One neighbor lost the path across the square and found it by striking a shield.
The storm buried steps, fences, and every track we might have followed.
Water went to coughing throats before it went to cleaning tools.
We kept the forge closed until the air stopped scraping our eyes.
The roofs held, though the west shutters need new hinges.
Morning left dunes against doors that opened freely yesterday.
Next time, every household gets cloth, water, and a line to the square.
Armor can wait on the stand. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the forge found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the forge. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing ice off the buckles and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the forge. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
We cleared the path to the forge before the snow could seal it again.
Frozen buckles are thawing beside bowls meant for cold hands.
We checked every quiet house for a hearth and an answer.
One shield made a decent shovel when the proper tools disappeared.
The wind erased tracks before we could trust where they led.
We moved spare coal to the homes farthest from the forge.
Armor stayed on the racks while we wrapped neighbors in every dry blanket.
The bell rope froze stiff, so we carried warnings door to door.
Ice locked two helmets shut until the wearers reached the hearth.
We marked the open paths with lanterns taller than the drifts.
Nobody crosses the farms alone until the whiteout passes.
The forge fire stayed low and steady so frightened people could gather safely.
A roof beam cracked under snow, but the family beneath it reached us in time.
Morning brought clear sky and a village full of shovels.
Before the next storm, every outer house gets fuel and a marked route inward.
I know which joint failed on the golem. Knowing does not make the square feel safer.
That iron protected us for years. It deserves more than being counted as scrap.
I gathered every piece before the children had to walk past it.
The village sounds wrong without those heavy steps at night.
We are counting iron, but we are also counting who now has to stand watch.
A cracked frame can be rebuilt. Trust takes longer at the anvil.
I found old dents from raids the golem never let reach our doors.
No one should melt that iron until the village agrees what comes next.
The poppies by the path look lonelier this morning.
I am drawing a stronger shoulder joint and hating why I need it.
The night watch doubled before sunset because our guardian will not make its rounds.
Some villagers want a replacement now. Others are not ready to look at one.
I cleaned the broken plates as if the golem might need them again.
Whoever rebuilds it should remember that protection is more than iron.
The square has room for those broad footsteps, and the empty space is hard to ignore.
We owe the farms, the bell, and several living neighbors to that fallen frame.
I will not pretend a new golem would be the same one.
Every recovered ingot carries a mark I recognize.
Tonight the forge stays lit while we plan the village's defense.
The golem stood between danger and people. Now we have to do the same.
